# S10 — blind re-derivation of the U/L/D instrument vs. the hand-built version

Three coders saw each O*NET element independently and assigned it to a cell (U = upward accountability, L = lateral service, D = downward command) or to nothing. Elements reaching 2-of-3 are treated as the blind pass's result. The hand-built instrument holds 19 elements (6 U, 5 L + the subtracted Realistic half, 7 D).

The blind pass placed **48 elements**: 10 in U, 17 in L, 21 in D. It re-derived **18 of the 19** hand-built elements, and nominated **30** the hand-built version does not contain.

## 1. CONFIRMED

Hand-built elements the blind pass independently put in the same cell.

**U — 5 of 6**

| ID | Name | Votes |
|---|---|---|
| 4.A.3.b.6 | Documenting/Recording Information | 3/3 |
| 4.A.4.a.2 | Communicating with Supervisors, Peers, or Subordinates | 3/3 (challenged, see §4) |
| 4.A.4.c.1 | Performing Administrative Activities | 3/3 |
| 4.C.3.a.4 | Freedom to Make Decisions | 3/3, reverse-scored 3/3 |
| 4.C.3.b.8 | Determine Tasks, Priorities and Goals | 3/3, reverse-scored 3/3 |

Both reverse-scorings were re-derived unanimously and for the stated reason (discretion is the inverse of answering upward). That is the least obvious design choice in the instrument and it survived a blind pass cleanly.

**L — 5 of 5, plus the composite's subtrahend**

| ID | Name | Votes |
|---|---|---|
| 4.A.4.a.3 | Communicating with People Outside the Organization | 3/3 |
| 4.A.4.a.4 | Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships | 3/3 |
| 4.A.4.a.5 | Assisting and Caring for Others | 3/3 |
| 4.A.4.a.8 | Performing for or Working Directly with the Public | 3/3 |
| 1.B.1.d | Social interest | 3/3 |
| 1.B.1.a | Realistic interest | 2/3, reverse-scored 2/2 |

The Social-minus-Realistic composite is effectively reproduced: Social lands in L unanimously, and the two coders who nominated Realistic both wanted it negative and both said in as many words that it is only meaningful as the subtracted half.

**D — 7 of 7**

| ID | Name | Votes |
|---|---|---|
| 4.A.4.b.1 | Coordinating the Work and Activities of Others | 3/3 |
| 4.A.4.b.3 | Training and Teaching Others | 3/3 (challenged, see §4) |
| 4.A.4.b.4 | Guiding, Directing, and Motivating Subordinates | 3/3 |
| 4.A.4.b.5 | Coaching and Developing Others | 3/3 |
| 4.A.4.c.2 | Staffing Organizational Units | 3/3 |
| 4.A.4.c.3 | Monitoring and Controlling Resources | 3/3 |
| 1.B.3.al | Management/Administration interest | 3/3 |

## 2. MISSED

Elements the blind pass placed that the hand-built instrument does not contain. Grouped by how seriously they should be taken, not by cell.

### 2a. Worth adding

Same measurement family as the existing instrument (Work Activities / Work Context), explicitly directional in the item text, 3/3, and not redundant with an element already in the cell.

| ID | Name | What it measures | Cell | Votes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4.C.1.c.2 | Work Outcomes and Results of Other Workers | Work Context: how responsible the worker is for other workers' outcomes | D | 3/3 |
| 4.C.1.b.1.f | Deal With External Customers or the Public in General | Work Context: importance of dealing with external customers or the public | L | 3/3 |
| 4.A.4.b.6 | Providing Consultation and Advice to Others | Activity: giving expert advice **to management** or other groups | U | 3/3 |

4.C.1.c.2 is the single cleanest downward indicator in O*NET — it asks directly about responsibility for other people's work — and the hand-built D contains no Work Context item at all. 4.C.1.b.1.f is its lateral twin and states the direction in the item stem, which almost nothing else does. 4.A.4.b.6 is the only activity element besides 4.A.4.a.2 that names a superior as the counterpart; U is the thin cell, and it is about to get thinner (§3).

### 2b. Defensible but marginal

Directionally plausible, but direction is inferred rather than stated, or the item is largely covered by something already in the cell.

| ID | Name | What it measures | Cell | Votes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4.A.4.a.7 | Resolving Conflicts and Negotiating with Others | Handling complaints, disputes, grievances | L | 3/3 |
| 4.A.4.a.6 | Selling or Influencing Others | Convincing others to buy or change their minds | L | 3/3 |
| 4.A.4.b.2 | Developing and Building Teams | Building trust and cooperation among team members | D | 3/3 |
| 4.C.1.b.1.g | Coordinate or Lead Others in Accomplishing Work Activities | Informal leading, explicitly *not* as supervisor | D | 3/3 |
| 4.A.2.b.5 | Scheduling Work and Activities | Scheduling events and "the work of others" | D | 3/3 |
| 4.A.2.b.4 | Developing Objectives and Strategies | Setting long-range objectives and strategies | U (reverse) | 2/3 |

The two L activity items name no counterpart; "team members" in 4.A.4.b.2 and the explicit non-supervisory clause in 4.C.1.b.1.g both point sideways as easily as down; 4.A.2.b.5 bundles scheduling your own work with scheduling others'. 4.A.2.b.4 is the interesting one conceptually — it is the organisation-level twin of the two reverse-scored autonomy items — but it reached only 2/3 and would make half of U reverse-scored discretion.

### 2c. Not worth adding

| ID | Name | Family | Cell | Votes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.C.1.a | Administration and Management | Knowledge | D | 3/3 |
| 2.C.1.f | Personnel and Human Resources | Knowledge | D | 3/3 |
| 2.C.6 | Education and Training | Knowledge | D | 3/3 |
| 2.C.1.e | Customer and Personal Service | Knowledge | L | 3/3 |
| 2.C.1.b | Administrative | Knowledge | U | 3/3 |
| 2.B.5.d | Management of Personnel Resources | Skill | D | 3/3 |
| 2.B.5.b | Management of Financial Resources | Skill | D | 3/3 |
| 2.B.5.c | Management of Material Resources | Skill | D | 3/3 |
| 2.B.1.f | Service Orientation | Skill | L | 3/3 |
| 2.B.1.e | Instructing | Skill | D | 2/3 |
| 1.D.1.i | Leadership Orientation | Work Style | D | 3/3 |
| 1.B.3.aj | Human Resources | Interest | D | 3/3 |
| 1.B.3.y | Teaching/Education | Interest | D | 3/3 |
| 1.B.3.ac | Personal Service | Interest | L | 3/3 |
| 1.B.3.z | Social Service | Interest | L | 3/3 |
| 1.B.3.ak | Office Work | Interest | U | 3/3 |
| 1.B.1.f | Conventional | Interest | U | 3/3 |
| 1.B.3.aa | Health Care Service | Interest | L | 2/3 |
| 1.B.3.ad | Professional Advising | Interest | L | 2/3 |
| 1.B.3.am | Public Speaking | Interest | L | 2/3 |
| 4.C.1.d.2 | Dealing With Unpleasant, Angry, or Discourteous People | Work Context | L | 3/3 |

Twenty-one of the thirty misses are Knowledge, Skill, Interest, or Work Style ratings — capacities and dispositions, not what the job requires the incumbent to do. The coders flagged nearly all of them as weak evidence themselves. They are also near-duplicates of activity elements already in the instrument (2.C.1.f shadows Staffing Organizational Units; 2.C.6 shadows Training and Teaching; 2.B.5.d shadows Guiding/Directing Subordinates; 2.C.1.a shadows the Management/Administration interest already in D). Adding them would multiply collinear measures of the same underlying thing and silently reweight the composite toward D — which is already the cell the blind pass over-nominates (21 elements vs. 10 for U).

Two specific warnings. First, the three non-activity U nominations (Conventional interest, Office Work interest, Administrative knowledge) all measure clerical and paperwork content. That is exactly the confound the challenge to Letters and Memos names (§4) — adding them would reimport through the back door the problem that dropping Letters and Memos is meant to remove. Second, 4.C.1.d.2 (angry people) indexes police and retail work, not the direction of an interaction; it would put occupational unpleasantness into a lateral-service score.

## 3. NOT RE-DERIVED

| ID | Name | Cell | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4.C.1.a.2.j | Written Letters and Memos | U | Nominated by **1 of 3** coders — below threshold. Not unmentioned: it was seen and rejected, and separately drew the largest set of seconded objections in the audit (7). |

That is the only hand-built element the blind pass failed to reproduce. Every other element was placed, in the right cell, by at least two of three coders.

Two other below-threshold nominations, for context, were elements *not* in the hand-built instrument: 4.C.1.b.1.e (Work With or Contribute to a Work Group or Team, L) and 4.C.3.a.2.b (Frequency of Decision Making, U), each 1 of 3.

## 4. CHALLENGED

| ID | Name | Seconds | Objection | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4.C.1.a.2.j | Written Letters and Memos | 7 | Two distinct problems. (i) No direction: the item asks only how *often* the job requires written correspondence; memos go to clients, the public, and subordinates as readily as to superiors. (ii) Circularity: it measures how writing-heavy a job is, and the outcome is a written bureaucratic register — a hit would say wordy jobs breed wordy speech, not that upward accountability does. This is the confound the hypothesis explicitly disclaims. | **Drop.** It failed the blind re-derivation *and* drew the heaviest objection; both point the same way. |
| 4.A.4.b.3 | Training and Teaching Others | 3 | The item does not specify who is taught. For teachers and nurses — occupations that matter in these chambers — the people instructed are students and patients served laterally, not subordinates commanded, so keeping it in D codes teachers as commanders. | **Keep in D, but test it.** It got 3/3 in D on blind coding, so the objection is a hypothesis, not a finding. Check empirically whether it loads with the supervisory D items or with L, and report the composite with it dropped as a robustness check. |
| 4.A.4.a.2 | Communicating with Supervisors, Peers, or Subordinates | 2 | One rating pools all three directions, so a pure supervisor scores high on it; it cannot separate upward from downward communication. | **Keep, downweight.** Both objectors concede nothing cleaner exists in O*NET, and it is the only activity element that names supervisors at all. Treat it as diluted evidence and say so in the write-up. |

## 5. Verdict

The hand-built instrument is substantially reproduced. Eighteen of nineteen elements came back in the same cell, and the two least obvious choices — the reverse-scored autonomy pair and the Social-minus-Realistic composite — were re-derived with their rationale intact. The single element that failed to reproduce is also the single most-objected-to element, which is convergent rather than coincidental. The blind pass is not evidence that the instrument should grow: three coders at 2-of-3 is weak evidence, most of what they added is a different kind of measurement, and thirty additions to nineteen elements would change what the instrument measures rather than measure it better.

Three changes worth making:

1. **Drop 4.C.1.a.2.j (Written Letters and Memos) from U.** Direction-free, and confounded with the outcome. This is the highest-value change in the audit.
2. **Add the two directional Work Context items:** 4.C.1.c.2 (Work Outcomes and Results of Other Workers) to D and 4.C.1.b.1.f (Deal With External Customers or the Public) to L. Both state the direction in the item stem, which almost nothing else in O*NET does, and both cells currently rely entirely on self-reported activity frequencies.
3. **Add 4.A.4.b.6 (Providing Consultation and Advice to Others) to U**, which keeps U at six elements after the drop and gives it a second item that names a superior as the recipient.

Everything else is noise or construct-widening. The Knowledge, Skill, Interest, and Work Style nominations should stay out: they are dispositions and capacities rather than job demands, they duplicate activity items already present, and they would tilt the composite toward D. The one thing the blind pass surfaces that no single edit fixes is that U is thin in O*NET generally — the coders found 21 downward elements and 10 upward ones, and half the upward ones are reverse-scored discretion. That is a limitation to state in the write-up, not something to paper over by adding weak items.
